questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: Persistent hoarseness of voice for more than three weeks in an adult smoker requires:
options: Urgent laryngoscopy to exclude carcinoma of the larynx
questions.concept: Hoarseness beyond three weeks is a red flag for laryngeal malignancy, especially in smokers, and mandates direct or flexible laryngoscopy. Glottic carcinoma presents early with hoarseness and has the best prognosis because of sparse lymphatics.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: The nerve most commonly injured during thyroidectomy causing hoarseness is:
options: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
questions.concept: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid; unilateral injury causes hoarseness with a paramedian cord, and bilateral injury causes stridor requiring tracheostomy. Injury to the external superior laryngeal branch causes loss of voice pitch.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: The only intrinsic muscle of the larynx that abducts the vocal cords is:
questions.concept: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor, opening the glottis for respiration; its paralysis therefore threatens the airway. All other intrinsic muscles adduct or tense the cords.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: Semon's law states that in a progressive lesion of the recurrent laryngeal nerve:
options: Abductor fibres are affected before adductor fibres
questions.concept: Semon's law describes earlier vulnerability of abductor fibres, so the cord first loses abduction and lies in a paramedian position; complete paralysis later allows it to drift to the cadaveric position with a breathy voice.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: The commonest cause of stridor in a neonate is:
questions.concept: Laryngomalacia causes inspiratory stridor worsening with feeding, crying and supine posture, from an omega-shaped epiglottis with floppy supraglottic tissue. Most resolve by 18 to 24 months; supraglottoplasty is rarely needed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: The site of election for tracheostomy is through tracheal rings:
questions.concept: The second and third rings are used: higher risks perichondritis and subglottic stenosis, and the cricoid must never be divided, while lower placement risks injury to the innominate vessels and a difficult tube change.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: Cricothyroidotomy is preferred over tracheostomy in an emergency because it is:
options: Quicker and technically easier through the readily palpable cricothyroid membrane
Less likely to cause subglottic stenosis
questions.concept: The cricothyroid membrane is superficial and easily palpable, allowing rapid access in a can't-intubate-can't-ventilate emergency. It is a temporary measure converted to formal tracheostomy within 24 to 48 hours, and is avoided in young children.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: Singer's nodules (vocal nodules) characteristically occur at:
options: The junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the vocal cord
questions.concept: This is the point of maximum vibratory contact during phonation, so chronic voice abuse produces bilateral symmetrical nodules. Treatment is voice rest and speech therapy, with surgery reserved for mature fibrotic nodules.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: Which laryngeal carcinoma has the best prognosis and why?
options: Glottic, because of early hoarseness and sparse lymphatic drainage
questions.concept: The glottis has almost no lymphatic drainage, so nodal spread is late, and even a small tumour causes hoarseness prompting early presentation. Supraglottic tumours present late with rich bilateral lymphatics and worse outcomes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Larynx: hoarseness, stridor, vocal cord palsy, tracheostomy
questions.stem: Bilateral abductor paralysis of the vocal cords presents with:
options: Stridor and dyspnoea with a good voice
questions.concept: Both cords lie in the paramedian position, so the voice is surprisingly preserved but the airway is critically narrowed, causing stridor on exertion and requiring tracheostomy or a cord lateralisation procedure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Ludwig angina is a cellulitis of the:
options: Bilateral submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually of dental origin
questions.concept: Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the floor of the mouth from a lower molar infection, elevating the tongue and threatening the airway. Airway protection, intravenous antibiotics and drainage are needed.
questions.reference: Dhingra ENT 7e, Deep Neck Space Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Retropharyngeal abscess in a child typically presents with:
options: Fever, dysphagia, torticollis and widened prevertebral soft tissue on lateral neck radiograph
questions.concept: Suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes after an upper respiratory infection in children under 5 causes fever, refusal to feed, neck stiffness and airway compromise, with prevertebral soft tissue widening on a lateral radiograph.
questions.reference: Dhingra ENT 7e, Deep Neck Space Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is distinguished from acute tonsillitis by:
options: Trismus with uvular deviation to the opposite side and a muffled hot-potato voice
questions.concept: Quinsy is a unilateral collection between the tonsillar capsule and superior constrictor, causing severe unilateral pain, trismus, drooling, a muffled voice and displacement of the uvula away from the affected side. Aspiration or incision with antibiotics is the treatment.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: An inhaled foreign body in a child most commonly lodges in the:
questions.concept: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so aspirated objects preferentially enter it. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: The commonest site of impaction of an ingested foreign body in the oesophagus is:
options: The cricopharyngeal sphincter at the level of C6
At the level of the aortic arch
questions.concept: The cricopharyngeus is the narrowest part of the alimentary tract and the commonest site of impaction; a coin lodged here appears in the coronal plane on an anteroposterior radiograph, whereas a tracheal coin appears sagittal.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: A button battery lodged in the oesophagus requires:
options: Emergency endoscopic removal because of rapid liquefactive necrosis
Oral fluids and repeat radiograph in a week
questions.concept: Button batteries generate an electrolytic current causing alkaline liquefactive necrosis and perforation within hours, so removal is a true emergency, distinct from smooth blunt objects which may be observed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: The parapharyngeal space infection classically causes:
options: Trismus with medial displacement of the lateral pharyngeal wall and tonsil
questions.concept: Infection in the parapharyngeal space pushes the tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall medially with trismus and neck swelling behind the angle of the jaw, and may involve the carotid sheath causing internal jugular thrombosis.
questions.reference: Dhingra ENT 7e, Deep Neck Space Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: Lemierre syndrome refers to:
options: Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with septic pulmonary emboli, usually from Fusobacterium
questions.concept: Following an oropharyngeal infection, Fusobacterium necrophorum causes internal jugular septic thrombophlebitis with metastatic septic emboli, most often to the lungs. Prolonged antibiotics with anaerobic cover are required.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love 28e, Head and Neck Infections

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: A midline neck swelling that moves upward on protrusion of the tongue is:
questions.concept: The thyroglossal duct remnant retains attachment to the hyoid and foramen caecum, so it rises on tongue protrusion and swallowing. Sistrunk operation removing the cyst with the central hyoid body prevents recurrence.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.topic: Neck spaces, deep neck infection & aerodigestive foreign bodies
questions.stem: A branchial cyst characteristically presents:
options: In the upper neck anterior to the sternocleidomastoid in a young adult
In the posterior triangle at birth
questions.concept: A second branchial cleft cyst lies deep to the anterior border of the upper third of sternocleidomastoid, presenting in the second or third decade, often enlarging after an upper respiratory infection, with cholesterol crystals in the aspirate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Healing of a clean surgical incision with apposed edges is termed:
questions.concept: Primary intention healing occurs when edges are approximated with minimal tissue loss, giving a fine scar. Secondary intention involves granulation and contraction across a gaping wound, and tertiary (delayed primary) closure follows a period of open management.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: The tensile strength of a healing wound at the end of one week is approximately what percentage of final strength?
questions.concept: Wound strength is only about 10% at one week, rising to 30% at three weeks and plateauing at 70 to 80% of original strength by three months - collagen remodelling continues but never restores full strength.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: A keloid differs from a hypertrophic scar in that it:
options: Extends beyond the original wound margins and rarely regresses
questions.concept: Keloids grow beyond the original wound boundary, recur after excision and are commoner in darker skin and over the sternum, shoulder and earlobe. Hypertrophic scars stay within the wound and often regress, especially across flexures after burns.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency most directly impairs collagen synthesis and wound healing?
questions.concept: Ascorbic acid is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen; deficiency gives weak collagen with wound dehiscence, bleeding gums and perifollicular haemorrhage. Zinc and protein deficiency also impair healing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: A clean-contaminated surgical wound is one in which:
options: The respiratory, alimentary or genitourinary tract is entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination
There is gross spillage of bowel contents
questions.concept: Wounds are classified clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated and dirty, with infection rates rising from under 2% to over 30%. Prophylactic antibiotics are indicated from the clean-contaminated class onward and in clean surgery involving implants.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Prophylactic antibiotic for a surgical procedure is best given:
options: At the time of skin closure
questions.concept: Timing to achieve peak tissue concentration at incision is critical; a single dose within 60 minutes before incision, repeated for long operations or major blood loss, is as effective as prolonged courses and reduces resistance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Which suture material is absorbable?
questions.concept: Polyglactin 910, polyglycolic acid, polydioxanone and catgut are absorbable, while silk, nylon, polypropylene and steel are non-absorbable. Absorbable sutures are used where removal is impractical, such as bowel and subcutaneous layers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Burst abdomen (abdominal wound dehiscence) classically presents:
options: Around the sixth to eighth postoperative day with serosanguinous salmon-coloured discharge
questions.concept: A pink serosanguinous discharge from the wound is the classic premonitory sign of impending dehiscence around day 6 to 8. Management is covering the wound with sterile saline packs and urgent resuture under anaesthesia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: The commonest cause of fever on the first postoperative day is:
options: Atelectasis or the inflammatory response to surgery
questions.concept: The classic sequence of postoperative fever is the five Ws: wind (atelectasis, days 1 to 2), water (urinary infection, days 3 to 5), wound (days 5 to 7), walking (venous thrombosis, days 5 to 7) and wonder drugs or abscess later.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Wound healing, surgical site infection & sutures
questions.stem: Negative pressure wound therapy promotes healing primarily by:
options: Removing exudate, reducing oedema and stimulating granulation tissue
questions.concept: Vacuum-assisted closure applies subatmospheric pressure that removes exudate, reduces interstitial oedema, increases local blood flow and mechanically stimulates granulation, useful in large contaminated or cavity wounds.
